newsitem.title: TUNISIA: Tunisia sees faster growth, lower inflation.
newsitem.headline: Tunisia sees faster growth, lower inflation.

text.p: The Tunisian economy, boosted by recovery from two years of drought, is benefitting from the triple blessings of rapid growth, falling inflation and a narrowing trade deficit.
Cereals output is sharply higher, phosphates production is expanding, and the revenues from olive oil and tourism are expected to reach record highs this year.
Government officials said growth in gross domestic product may reach 7.5 to 8.0 percent in 1996, compared with an earlier budget forecast of 6.7 percent, and only 2.5 percent in 1995.
Annual inflation, measured by the consumer price index, was down to 4.0 percent in the first nine months of 1996 compared with 6.3 percent for the same period last year, they said.

The trade deficit for the first eight months of 1996 fell to 1.43 billion dinars ($1.47 billion) from 1.58 billion dinars during the same period last year, official figures obtained by Reuters but still to be released showed.

Economic Development Minister Taoufik Baccar said that based on an estimated 2.5 million tonnes cereals crop, the growth rate would be 7.5 percent, and up to 8.0 percent if the crop was larger. The Agriculture Ministry has yet to release crop figures.
GDP growth rate was 2.5 percent in 1995 and 3.3 percent in 1994, partly because drought reduced the cereals harvest to 0.62 million tonnes in 1995 and 0.65 million tonnes in 1994.
The upward revision in growth estimates was also partly due to improved production and exports of phosphates and phosphates by-products, a Central Bank report said.

Exports of the chemical sector, mainly by-products of phosphates of which Tunisia is one of the world's largest exporters, rose by 17.5 percent during the first eight months of 1996, but details of shipments were not disclosed.

The agriculture sector, which usually accounts for around 16 percent of GDP and 11 percent of exports earnings and employs one-third of the labour force, is highly vulnerable to irregular rainfall patterns.
Baccar said that because of drought, the average GDP growth rate during the five-year 1992-1996 development plan was estimated at 4.6 percent per year, less than the average six percent goal.
Agriculture sector output fell an average 1.7 percent a year during the period, compared with a goal of 2.0 percent growth.

Other recent good news for the Tunisian economy includes the prospects for record production of olive oil, of which Tunisia is a leading world exporter, and an expected increase in tourism revenues, one of Tunisia's important sources of foreign currency.
Unofficial estimates put the olive oil production at a 220,000 tonnes, from only 60,000 tonnes last year. Tourism revenues are expected to reach a record 1.4 billion dinars. ($=0.97 dinar)
